newsitem.title: UK: Euro pump prices stay firm despite crude oil plunge.
newsitem.headline: Euro pump prices stay firm despite crude oil plunge.

text.p: European motorists have yet to feel the benefit of a three-month, 30 percent slump in world crude oil values with pump prices showing little change since the start of the year, oil analysts say.

But industry experts believe oil companies are not making a killing. Increased local taxes and duties and the soaring value of the dollar, the oil trade's business currency, are to blame for stubbornly high retail prices.
"It's not surprising anyone in this business that product prices are not falling in line with crude," said Peter Bogin, of Cambridge Energy Research Associates.

Benchmark Brent crude prices have fallen from just under $25 a barrel in early January to $18 now, with runaway production pushing a glut of oil on to the market and a mild winter cutting into demand.
Oil product prices have slipped in line with crude, although seasonal consumption patterns skew the picture, with more gasoline and less diesel oil used in the summer.
A barrel of premium unleaded gasoline costs around $22.70 a barrel, $4 less than in late December, while diesel fuel has plummeted from around $29 a barrel to just over $20.

But figures from the European Commission and independent analysts suggest that motorists everywhere but in Britain are paying broadly as much, if not more, for their gasoline as they did at the end of last year.

According to researchers Oil Price Assessments Ltd (OPAL), it cost a motorist 2.03 guilders ($1.05) for a litre of unleaded gasoline in the Netherlands at the end of December. In early April a litre cost 2.04 guilders.
European Commission figures, taking into account a recent price cut, put the cost at 2.03 guilders. A similar pattern emerges in Germany, Spain and Italy, OPAL says.
Truck owners filling up with diesel have been more fortunate, seeing price dips in a range from 1.7 percent in France to over 3.5 percent in Belgium and Spain.

But these cuts and recent announcements of retail reductions in gasoline, due to political and competitive pressure, in Italy, Spain and the Netherlands, are minor compared to the fall in wholesale prices.
The problem is the dollar, analysts say, which has risen by over 10 percent against mainland European currencies this year and eaten away at the benefits of crude's fall.
The U.S. currency on Wednesday hit a two-year high against the mark.
Tax and duty, which typically account for around 70 percent of fuel's retail price in Europe, also rose.
"We are now seeing a declining price trend everywhere but it would have been much larger were it not for the dollar," said OPAL's director Peter Regnier.

Analysts say that the oil majors, struggling for profit in a crowded refining market, are seeking growth in the retail sector. The increased competition prevents most from making windfall profits out of the fall in crude, they say.

Supermarkets have forced prices down in France and Britain, winning substantial market share, and now threaten in eastern Germany, Spain and Portugal, while low-cost entrants have taken five percent of Scandinavia's market in two years.
In Britain, where sterling has risen in step with the dollar, fuel prices have fallen some 2.5 percent this year.
While crude's fall has not made retailing lucrative in Britain, there is a suggestion oil companies are using it to build some breadth back into margins squeezed wafer-thin by last year's price wars.

"Margins last year went to levels that were not viable in the long term," said an Esso spokesman in Britain. "In some markets retailing was unprofitable and clearly that is not tenable for any business."
($ = 1.930 Dutch Guilders)
